To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

students’ perception of their responsibilities in a language classroom in East Asia is influenced by their beliefs about the nature of language learning and teaching, and that their beliefs about the role of teachers, learners and the language classroom are influenced by their culture.

students’ perception of their own responsibilities in a language classroom is affected by the teacher’s role in promoting student autonomy, the teacher’s attitude towards student autonomy, and the students’ perception of the teacher’s attitude.

the majority of the participants were satisfied with their English classes, that the majority of them felt that the teachers were responsible for their learning, and that most of them were satisfied with the amount of autonomy they had in their classes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the extent to which students take responsibility for their own language learning.
the extent to which students are willing to assume responsibility for their own learning.
the question of how learners can be helped to take greater responsibility for their learning, and how they can learn how to learn.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

learner autonomy is the ability to take responsibility for one’s own learning and development as a learner, and that this involves the ability to make decisions about learning and the willingness to act upon them.
autonomy in language learning is an ability of learners to take charge of their own learning in the classroom and beyond.
learner autonomy is a complex concept that has been defined and conceptualized in various ways.

autonomy is a self-regulatory process in which the individual takes the initiative for his or her own learning in collaboration with others.

the term learner autonomy has come to refer to a set of beliefs and practices which are intended to promote the development of independent, self-directed learners, and that these are based on the assumption of the learner as a responsible participant in his or her learning process (Littlewood, 1999, p71) The concept of learner autonomy has been discussed by many researchers and teachers, but there has been little research on the perceptions and responsibilities of students in East Asian classrooms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the students in this study have been given opportunities to take responsibility for their learning.
students in East Asian contexts have a different view of what it means to be autonomous.
students’ autonomy is not a fixed state but a process that is influenced by many factors, including teachers’ beliefs and practices and the social and cultural context.
